records.title: Remotion
records.summary: A React framework for video. Each frame is a component rendered from the frame number; the CLI renders the frames in headless Chrome and encodes MP4.
records.why_it_matters: The most established code renderer an agent can drive locally, and the one most skills target. Its licence is the first thing to check before company work.
records.fit_notes: Free for a person or a company of up to 3 employees; a bigger company needs a paid Company License, and the FAQ adds a per-render plan for automations (code that calls renderMedia() and similar). The repo says a changed licence ships with Remotion 5.0 (PR #3750); re-read LICENSE.md when you upgrade. For agent feedback, `npx remotion still <entry> <id> out.png --frame=N` gives one PNG without a full render, and `npx remotion render <id> out/frames --frames=0,30,90 --image-format=png` gives several (v4.0.502+). Animations written with CSS keyframes or setTimeout flicker or freeze because tabs render frames out of order.

related.note: Kinetograph states it renders Remotion projects without a browser.

claims.text: The free licence covers individuals, for-profit companies with up to 3 employees, non-profits and evaluation; others need a Company License.
claims.quote: a for-profit organization with up to 3 employees

claims.text: A single frame can be rendered to an image from the CLI, which gives an agent a frame to inspect before the full render.
claims.quote: Render a still frame based on the entry point, the composition ID and save it to the output location.

claims.text: CSS animations and timers are not captured correctly because frames render independently and out of order.
claims.quote: Remotion renders each frame independently. Frame 30 might be rendered before frame 10, or frame 50 might be rendered twice.

checked.what: LICENSE.md, license/faq.mdx, cli/still.mdx and troubleshooting/css-animations.mdx against the claims

records.title: Manim Community Edition
records.summary: A Python animation engine for explanatory math video, forked from 3b1b/manim in 2020 and run by a community team. The `manim` CLI renders a Scene class to a video file.
records.why_it_matters: The usual route for diagram and equation animation written by an agent in Python, with a one-flag way to get the last frame as a PNG.
records.fit_notes: `manim -s` (or `--format=png`) writes only the last frame, and `-ql` renders at low quality; both cut the review loop for an agent. Install needs system packages (the README points to per-OS docs; LaTeX only for TeX). The README says a major refactor is in progress, so APIs may move. Do not mix its install steps with 3b1b/manim: the package names differ and both READMEs warn of breakage.

related.note: Fork of it; different package and CLI.

claims.text: It is the community-maintained fork of 3b1b/manim, and its maintainers recommend it over the original.
claims.quote: It was forked from 3b1b/manim, a tool originally created and open-sourced by Grant Sanderson

claims.text: The CLI can skip the animation and save only the final frame as a PNG.
claims.quote: -s, --save_last_frame          Fast-forward animations and save the last frame
claims.locator: docs.manim.community, Configuration guide, command line help

claims.text: Using the other project's install instructions breaks the install.
claims.quote: Trying to use these instructions to install [3b1b/manim](https://github.com/3b1b/manim) or instructions there to install this version will cause problems.

checked.what: README.md and the docs configuration guide against the claims

records.title: ManimGL (3b1b/manim)
records.summary: Grant Sanderson's own Manim, installed as `manimgl`. It plays scenes in an OpenGL window and writes a file with `-w`.
records.why_it_matters: The original engine behind 3Blue1Brown videos. An agent that writes ManimCE code for it, or the reverse, gets errors, so the reader must pick one.
records.fit_notes: On a Mac it needs FFmpeg and, on ARM, Cairo from Homebrew; LaTeX is optional (MacTeX is about 6 GB, BasicTeX is the README's lighter path). The default run opens a window for a person; an agent needs `-w` to write a file or `-so` to save the final frame. Fewer tests and docs than ManimCE by its own README's account.

claims.text: Its README says the community edition was forked to be more stable, better tested and easier to start with.
claims.quote: In 2020 a group of developers forked it into what is now the [community edition](https://github.com/ManimCommunity/manim/), with a goal of being more stable, better tested, quicker to respond to community contributions, and all around friendlier to get started with.

claims.text: The pip package is manimgl, not manim.
claims.quote: The package name is `manimgl` instead of `manim` or `manimlib`.

claims.text: A flag saves the final frame as an image, which an agent can inspect.
claims.quote: `-so` will save the final frame to an image and show it

checked.what: README.md against the claims and against the ManimCE README

records.title: Motion Canvas
records.summary: A TypeScript library that programs vector animation with generators, plus a browser editor with live preview. Rendering is started from the editor.
records.why_it_matters: Good for code explainers synced to voice-over, but its render step is a button in a browser editor, which an agent cannot press without browser automation.
records.fit_notes: For an agent that must produce the MP4 itself, use Revideo, its fork with a headless render API. The default exporter writes an image sequence; MP4 needs the FFmpeg exporter. Snapshots of the current frame go to /still in the output folder, again from the editor. I did not check for a documented headless or CLI render path beyond the rendering page.

related.note: Revideo is forked from Motion Canvas and adds headless rendering.

claims.text: It is a generator-based TypeScript library plus an editor for real-time preview, aimed at vector animation synced to voice-over.
claims.quote: It's a specialized tool designed to create informative vector animations and synchronize them with voice-overs.

claims.text: Rendering starts from the RENDER button in the editor, which plays through the animation.
claims.quote: Clicking the RENDER button will initialize rendering

claims.text: Without an extra exporter the output is an image sequence, not a video.
claims.quote: If you don't see this option, it means that you don't have any additional exporters installed and the default Image sequence exporter will be used.

checked.what: README.md and the docs Rendering page against the claims

records.title: Revideo
records.summary: A TypeScript engine for video in code, forked from Motion Canvas, with a headless renderVideo() API and a React player for preview. It renders through Node and a headless browser.
records.why_it_matters: It gives the Motion Canvas authoring model a render call an agent can run, and it names Claude and Codex as authors.
records.fit_notes: The repo moved from redotvideo/revideo to midrender/revideo and is the engine behind the Midrender product. It counts renders through PostHog unless you set DISABLE_TELEMETRY=true. The README says it borrows from Remotion and Rive while its docs say it is a Motion Canvas fork; both can be true, but expect Motion Canvas APIs. I did not find a documented single-frame still command in what I read.

claims.text: Its README names Claude and Codex as able to write a scene, because a scene is plain TypeScript.
claims.quote: A scene is plain TypeScript, so Claude or Codex can produce one from a prompt.

claims.text: Headless rendering runs wherever Node and a headless browser run.
claims.quote: It runs anywhere Node and a headless browser run

claims.text: It anonymously counts rendered videos and can be switched off with an environment variable.
claims.quote: Revideo anonymously counts how many videos are rendered

checked.what: README.md and the docs welcome page against the claims

records.title: html-video
records.summary: A local studio and CLI that has a coding agent write animated HTML frames from a prompt, article or repo, then renders them to MP4 through the HyperFrames engine.
records.why_it_matters: A wrapper that drives Claude Code or Codex as a subprocess and ships 21 templates; only the HyperFrames engine works so far.
records.fit_notes: Needs Node 20+, pnpm, ffmpeg and Playwright Chromium. Remotion, Motion Canvas, Revideo and Manim adapters are planned, not built. It runs some agents with permission-skipping flags (`--yolo`, `--allow-all-tools`); check what it launches before use. Optional soundtrack needs a paid MiniMax key. Its engine table says Remotion is paid above 4 devs, which differs from Remotion's own licence text (free up to 3 employees).

claims.text: Only the HyperFrames engine renders today; the other engines are on the roadmap.
claims.quote: Remotion, Motion Canvas / Revideo, and Manim are on the roadmap: the adapter interface is designed for them, but their adapters aren't built yet.
claims.locator: README.md, Why this exists, Status note

claims.text: It invokes some agent CLIs with flags that skip permission prompts.
claims.quote: `copilot --allow-all-tools`, prompt via stdin
claims.locator: README.md, Supported agents, GitHub Copilot CLI row

claims.text: Its engine table describes Remotion's licence as paid above 4 developers.
claims.quote: Source-available, paid above 4 devs
claims.locator: README.md, Why this exists, engine table, Remotion row

checked.what: README.md against the claims and against Remotion LICENSE.md

records.title: fframes
records.summary: A Rust framework where each frame is an SVG tree returned by a function, drawn with Skia on the GPU and encoded with statically linked FFmpeg libraries. It ships a skill and a preview window with scrubbing.
records.why_it_matters: A browser-free renderer aimed at agent iteration speed. Its speed claim against Remotion is the vendor's own and unmeasured here.
records.fit_notes: Needs Rust and, on macOS, `brew install pkg-config ffmpeg x264 x265 opus nasm ninja`; the first build downloads prebuilt Skia and FFmpeg for macOS arm64. The agent writes Rust, so compile errors are part of the loop. The skill installs from a remote site (`npx skills add https://fframes.studio`); read it before installing. `cargo run --release -- preview` opens a window for a person; I did not find a documented still-frame command for the agent.

claims.text: The project claims to render more than 30 times faster than Remotion.
claims.quote: we are over 30x faster than remotion

claims.text: A missing font falls back silently in the render; the inspect command reports it and the fix is to put the font file in media/.
claims.quote: **Text renders in the wrong font:** `inspect` reports `No match for ... font-family`; put the font file in the

claims.text: Its skill installs from the project's website rather than from the repo.
claims.quote: npx skills add https://fframes.studio

downgrade.note: The speed claim is the vendor's own benchmark against a competitor.

records.title: Kinetograph
records.summary: A browser-free video engine: Node runs a Remotion-style TSX or HTML project and a Rust GPU compositor draws each frame. It states that Remotion and HyperFrames projects render unchanged.
records.why_it_matters: It could give Remotion or HyperFrames code a render path with no Chrome, and its docs list in detail what it cannot draw. The repo was created on 2026-10-23 and is in beta.
records.fit_notes: Prebuilt package for macOS on Apple Silicon, Node 22+. `kinetograph doctor <entry>` lists every unsupported element and frame before a long render, and `--strict` fails the render instead of drawing an approximation; use both in agent loops. It reads no system fonts: CJK, Arabic and Devanagari draw as boxes unless you load a font. Compatibility claims against Remotion and HyperFrames are the author's; not measured here. Running it on Remotion code does not change what Remotion's licence asks of you; I did not check that question.

claims.text: It renders without a browser, using a Rust GPU compositor, and states that Remotion and HyperFrames projects render as they are.
claims.quote: Existing Remotion projects render as they are, and so do

claims.text: A doctor command checks every frame without the GPU and lists what cannot be drawn, before a long render.
claims.quote: kinetograph doctor <entry> goes through every frame without the GPU and lists what can't be drawn, on which frames, and any scene a render would refuse.

claims.text: Its docs admit rare non-identical output between GPU renders at the same settings, and give a bit-exact fallback.
claims.quote: Rarely, when renderers share the GPU, two renders at the same concurrency differ by 1 in one colour channel on a few pixels of a frame.

checked.what: README.md and the docs Compatibility page against the claims

records.title: FFmpeg
records.summary: The command-line encoder and filter engine under almost every renderer here. Filtergraphs alone can cross-fade clips (xfade), burn in text (drawtext) and normalise loudness (loudnorm).
records.why_it_matters: An agent can finish or assemble a clip with FFmpeg alone, and most render failures that reach the reader are FFmpeg input mismatches.
records.fit_notes: xfade fails unless both inputs share resolution, pixel format, frame rate and timebase: scale and fps-normalise first. loudnorm defaults to -24 LUFS integrated; set I= to the platform target yourself. drawtext exists only if your build was configured with libfreetype and libharfbuzz; run `ffmpeg -filters | grep drawtext` before relying on it. I did not check which flags the Homebrew build enables.

claims.text: xfade needs both inputs to match in frame rate, resolution, pixel format and timebase.
claims.quote: Both inputs must be constant frame-rate and have the same resolution, pixel format, frame rate and timebase.

claims.text: loudnorm defaults to an integrated loudness target of -24.
claims.quote: Range is -70.0 - -5.0. Default value is -24.0.

claims.text: drawtext is only compiled in when FFmpeg is configured with libfreetype and libharfbuzz.
claims.quote: To enable compilation of this filter, you need to configure FFmpeg with --enable-libfreetype and --enable-libharfbuzz.

checked.what: ffmpeg-filters.html sections xfade, loudnorm and drawtext against the claims

records.title: editly
records.summary: A Node.js tool that builds a video from a JSON5 edit spec of clips, images, titles, audio and GL transitions, streaming through ffmpeg.
records.why_it_matters: A declarative format an agent can write without a frame model, with a `--fast` flag for a low-cost preview render.
records.fit_notes: Needs ffmpeg and ffprobe on PATH and a native headless-gl build; the README's troubleshooting is mostly native-module errors. Without `--fast`, every clip is converted to the first input's size and frame rate, which surprises mixed inputs. The last push to the repo was 2025-05-12 (GitHub API, read 2026-11-12), so I marked it dormant. It is a single-maintainer project by its README.

claims.text: Its fast mode renders at low resolution and frame rate for a quick preview.
claims.quote: Fast mode (low resolution and FPS, useful for getting a quick preview ⏩)
claims.locator: README.md, Edit spec options table, fast

claims.text: Without fast mode, output size and frame rate come from the first input video.
claims.quote: Without `--fast`, it will default to using the **width**, **height** and **frame rate** from the **first** input video.
claims.locator: README.md, Usage: Command line video editor

claims.text: It needs ffmpeg and ffprobe installed and on PATH.
claims.quote: `ffmpeg` (and `ffprobe`) [installed](http://ffmpeg.org/) and available in `PATH`

checked.what: README.md against the claims; push date from the GitHub API

records.title: MoviePy
records.summary: A Python library for cutting, compositing and titling video. It loads frames as numpy arrays and encodes the result through ffmpeg.
records.why_it_matters: Easy for an agent to script in Python, but agent training data is full of v1 code that v2 broke.
records.fit_notes: Tell the agent to target MoviePy v2 and to read the v1-to-v2 guide: its README example uses v2 names such as `subclipped` and `with_volume_scaled`, and code written against v1 docs fails. It is slower than ffmpeg alone, so use it for logic and let ffmpeg do heavy filters. TextClip takes a font file path, so ship the .ttf with the project. The README asks for maintainers. I did not check a still-frame API.

claims.text: Version 2.0 introduced major breaking changes and v1 is no longer maintained.
claims.quote: MoviePy recently upgraded to v2.0, introducing major breaking changes.

claims.text: Its own README says it is slower than using ffmpeg directly.
claims.quote: albeit slower than using ffmpeg directly due to heavier data import/export operations

records.title: MCP for Blender
records.summary: A third-party MCP server and Blender add-on that lets an agent run Python in a live Blender, look at viewport, camera and animation-strip views, and render. Blender itself renders headless with `blender -b file.blend -a`.
records.why_it_matters: The working path for 3D shots driven by an agent, with a built-in way for the agent to see its own frames.
records.fit_notes: The server runs any Python the agent writes inside Blender by default; set BLENDER_MCP_SAFE_MODE=1 and save your .blend first. The quick start pipes a remote script to sh; the manual setup avoids that. Some 3D-generation features are premium or need Sketchfab or Hyper3D keys. For the final video, the agent can call Blender's own CLI (`blender -b file.blend -a`, with -f N for one frame); put -o and format flags before -a.

claims.text: Its tool for running code executes arbitrary Python in Blender, and the README tells you to save your work first.
claims.quote: The `execute_blender_code` tool allows running arbitrary Python code in Blender, which can be powerful but potentially dangerous.

claims.text: A look tool returns viewport, camera, multi-angle or animation-strip views so the agent can check a frame.
claims.quote: See the result from the `viewport`, `camera`, `angles` (auto-framed multi-view sheet, any direction) or `frames` (animation strip)

claims.text: Blender's CLI renders without the UI, and argument order matters: -f or -a must come last.
claims.quote: Always position -f or -a as the last arguments.
claims.locator: docs.blender.org, Rendering From The Command Line

checked.what: README.md and the Blender manual command-line render page against the claims

records.title: GSAP
records.summary: A JavaScript animation library, owned by Webflow, that HyperFrames uses for motion and Remotion projects can seek. It has no renderer of its own; a frame-seeking renderer captures it.
records.why_it_matters: Most HTML video an agent writes moves with GSAP, so its licence travels with every HyperFrames clip.
records.fit_notes: Commercial use costs nothing, including the plugins that used to be paid. The licence is not open source: it bans use in no-code visual animation builders that compete with Webflow, and Webflow can change the terms by posting new ones. A renderer must pause and seek GSAP timelines per frame; a tween left playing on the wall clock is what breaks HyperFrames and Remotion renders.

claims.text: Commercial use is covered at no charge, including formerly members-only plugins such as SplitText and MorphSVG.
claims.quote: Commercial usage is covered under the standard license.

claims.text: Use inside no-code visual animation tools that compete with Webflow is prohibited.
claims.quote: "Prohibited Uses" means any implementation and/or use of GSAP Products in tools that allow users to build visual animations without code that encourages, induces, or materially assists in creating a solution that competes with Webflow’s visual animation building capabilities.

claims.text: AI-generated GSAP code is stated not to be a prohibited use.
claims.quote: AI-generated code is not a "Prohibited Use".

checked.what: gsap.com/standard-license (effective 2025-04-30, modified 2025-05-30) and README.md against the claims
